stories.headline: India extends ₹15,000 crore to Nepal for post-flood reconstruction
stories.title: India extends ₹15,000 crore to Nepal for post-flood reconstruction
stories.summary: PM Modi says assistance will “strengthen” Nepal’s dealing with natural disasters; India will have a “forward-looking approach” on border issues, says Foreign Secretary
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

opening: PM Modi says assistance will “strengthen” Nepal’s dealing with natural disasters; India will have a “forward-looking approach” on border issues, says Foreign Secretary.

New Delhi, Nov 23: New Delhi on Monday announced a development assistance package of Rs 15,000 crore for Nepal, including Rs 3,500 crore in grants for post-disaster reconstruction and infrastructure projects and a Rs 11,500-crore line of credit for energy sector projects.
body: The announcement was made during talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah, who was on his first State Visit to India since assuming office.

The two Prime Ministers also adopted a Joint Vision for a “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal”, laying out an ambitious roadmap to strengthen bilateral cooperation in areas ranging from economic development, connectivity and energy to digital services, space, innovation and disaster management.
PM Modi reaffirmed India’s unwavering support for Nepal’s development journey, describing the neighbouring country as a close friend.
Nepal Prime Minister Shah, in turn, appreciated India’s humanitarian and technical assistance following the devastating Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi floods in Nepal.
The assistance package includes Rs 3,500 crore in grant assistance (NPR 5,600 crore) and a rupee-denominated line of credit of Rs 11,500 crore (NPR 18,400 crore).
Specific projects and modalities will be finalised through mutual consultations.
Connectivity emerged as a major focus of the discussions, with PM Modi announcing a new transit trade route for Nepal through Deendayal Port at Kandla in Gujarat.
Access to Paradip Port in Odisha will also be provided once the required infrastructure is in place.
The two sides agreed to make the existing Kathmandu-Bhairahawa-Lucknow B345 air route bidirectional, with technical consultations to finalise the arrangements.
India and Nepal also finalised the Field Location Survey for the proposed Raxaul-Kathmandu electrified broad-gauge railway line.
They agreed to collaborate in developing Nepal’s East-West Railway.
The two Prime Ministers virtually laid the foundation stone for a new Integrated Check Post (ICP) at Banbasa and welcomed progress on similar facilities at Bhairahawa, Sunauli and Dodhara-Chandani.
A new motorable bridge connecting Dharchula in India with Darchula in Nepal was also inaugurated to improve cross-border connectivity.
In the energy sector, the leaders dedicated Phase II of the Motihari-Amlekhgunj petroleum pipeline to the people of Nepal and virtually laid the foundation stone for a petroleum terminal at Jhapa.
They stressed the need for an early start to work on the Siliguri-Jhapa pipeline and agreed to explore cooperation in developing gas pipelines.
The two sides also welcomed progress in hydropower cooperation and the participation of Indian companies in Nepal’s energy sector.
The leaders virtually laid the foundation stone for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project.

They directed the Pancheshwar Development Authority and the Joint Committee on Water Resources to expedite the finalisation of the Detailed Project Report of the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project and begin its implementation.
Work on the DPRs of the Saptakoshi and Sunkoshi multipurpose projects will also be accelerated to utilise water resources and mitigate floods.
The two countries also reviewed progress towards setting up joint ventures for two high-capacity cross-border transmission lines connecting Inaruwa-New Purnea and Dododhara-Bareilly.
In the education sector, India agreed to establish an offshore IIT campus in Nepal to strengthen technical education and promote employment opportunities.
The two leaders welcomed expanding cooperation in technology, start-ups and digital and financial connectivity.
They also emphasised the need to facilitate easier access to banking and telecom services for citizens of one country living in the other.

Eight memoranda of understanding were exchanged during the visit, covering cooperation in forensic sciences, police training, civil service capacity-building, traditional medicine, satellite communication, sustainable urban development, healthcare, and livestock and fisheries development.
The two leaders also reviewed progress in ongoing development projects, including High Impact Community Development Projects and the construction of Nepal’s National.
Police Academy with Indian assistance.
They welcomed the announcement of an Agro-Industrial Park in Chitwan, to be established with Indian grant assistance.

On the boundary issue, the leaders noted progress in joint fieldwork for the maintenance and repair of boundary pillars and directed their Foreign Secretaries to work towards resolving outstanding boundary issues.
Shah also called on President Droupadi Murmu and paid homage to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar called on the visiting Prime Minister.
Shah thanked PM Modi for the hospitality extended to him and his delegation and invited him to visit Nepal.
Modi accepted the invitation, with dates to be finalised through diplomatic channels.

bullets.text: The leaders also flagged off the inaugural Sarayu-Kamala Express rail service between Ayodhya and Janakpur, a move expected to boost religious and cultural tourism along the Ramayana Circuit and strengthen civilisational ties between the two countries.

stories.headline: Election petitions filed challenging bypoll victory of two TVK MLAs
stories.title: Election petitions filed challenging bypoll victory of two TVK MLAs
stories.summary: Dharapuram AIADMK candidate Banumathi and Madurantakam constituency voter S. Umapathi have filed the election petitions
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Two election petitions have been filed in the Madras High Court challenging the victory of TVK MLAs P. Sathyabama and Maragatham Kumaravel from Dharapuram and Madurantakam constituencies respectively in the byelections held for the two constituencies in October 2026.
The election petitions have been filed by Dharapuram AIADMK candidate K. Banumathi and Madurantakam constituency voter S. Umapathi.
Ms. Sathyabama and Ms. Kumaravel had won the byelections by securing 66,841 and 74,048 votes respectively.

The bypolls were necessitated because of the resignation of the two MLAs who had initially won from the same constituencies during the general elections held in April-May this year as AIADMK candidates but tendered their resignations to Speaker J.C.D. Prabhakar before joining TVK.

stories.headline: SCO civilisational dialogue
stories.title: SCO civilisational dialogue
stories.summary: India hosted the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in Delhi. To my mind, this is one of the most important and momentous events in recent years, surpassing other summits and their deliberations. The word “civilizational” has a special meaning for Indians. When I say Indians, I speak of the unity of thought and action in diversity, which moves beyond borders. Civilizational values are never restricted to geographical boundaries—that is the very essence of values derived from our heritage and landscape. The Civilisational Dialogue event offered a comprehensive look at a governance model shaped by a rich heritage—one that has guided the lives of ordinary people for centuries—alongside the challenges it faces in the future. This reflects distinct historical phases of India’s transformation and the spread of its values across the region. While the SCO served as a starting point, the broader goal is universal: advancing the ideal that the entire world is one family. It was more than appropriate for India to host the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. The idea was mooted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Tianjin, China, in 2025, and was later formally adopted at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan in September this year. The PM’s idea took off in a big way at Purana Qila, a historic fort epitomizing the centuries-old cultural ethos of the country, from a time when its influence extended across areas that now fall within the political maps of neighboring countries, particularly Pakistan and Bangladesh. It also draws our attention to China, a civilization that has progressed all along. The civilizational convergence between India and China defines their relationship more than anything else. The mountains and the Silk Route passing through these heights are things that storms and quakes have not been able to erase. In India’s context, Allama Iqbal’s poem Sare Jahan Se Accha Hindustan Hamara is a timeless narration of our heritage, particularly the lines: These lines say that we have something within ourselves that has allowed us to survive as a civilization, even though the cycle of time has been our enemy for centuries. In his inaugural address welcoming the delegates to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Prime Minister Narendra Modi drew a contrast between the current world order and the timing of India hosting this dialogue: “At a time when discussions around the world are dominated by war and unrest, we are holding a dialogue in India on civilizational connections. This is especially important because cultural connection is the strongest guarantee of global peace.” This was a thought-provoking exposition. It was also an invocation to the world—especially SCO members, including China and Pakistan—to rediscover our heritage and connect it to posterity using technology and high-speed connectivity. Technological advancement is now part of the civilizational journey; it has enhanced the scale of understanding, provided the true spirit is invoked and honored. The essence of his message was not to throw history out the window, but rather to open windows to our shared heritage and build upon the pillars of the past so they become a beacon for a future of peace and promise. This was further reinforced when PM Modi said: “Only a few months ago, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation completed 25 years of its establishment. Over the years, the SCO has significantly expanded cooperation in security, economy, and connectivity. In such a situation, cultural and civilizational cooperation will further strengthen relations among different countries. I am confident that this forum will generate new ideas, create new opportunities for cultural cooperation, and that our shared civilizational experiences will play an important role in bringing the world together.” This is not an easy task given the tough conditions across the world. The global order is in turmoil, where wars are driving divisive narratives and communities are becoming bitter enemies. Many of the gains of the post-World War II era are being lost. At this hour, speaking of civilizational dialogue and its importance in the pursuit of peace marks an epoch-making turn in history. It has opened a window to the future, provided we seize it and keep it open. As the PM stated in the clearest terms, the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum is not merely a ceremonial platform; it can become a platform for giving direction to the world. Modi offered several suggestions on advancing a new relationship between heritage and future prospects, as well as what new generations can do in this direction. He spoke of opportunities for cultural exchange, joint museum exhibitions, and exchange programs between universities and research institutions for scholars and researchers. He also emphasized the importance of cultural tourism, stating: “Cultural tourism can also become an important area of cooperation among us. Many historical sites linked to the Silk Routes and Buddhist heritage exist across our countries. We can explore possibilities for connecting them through heritage circuits and cultural routes. Similarly, joint cultural festivals and artists’ exchange programmes can bring our art and cultural traditions to new audiences. I believe such efforts will give our citizens better opportunities to understand each other’s cultures more closely. The responsibility for taking forward this civilizational dialogue that we are advancing today to even greater heights in the coming decades rests with our youth. Today’s younger generation is connected through technology and wants to understand the world better. We must provide more opportunities for our youth to connect with each other’s languages, literature, and cultural traditions. Our young artists, writers, and filmmakers can take our shared heritage to future generations through digital media and other creative platforms. We must also connect local artists and artisans to these efforts.” If followed in letter and spirit with sincerity, these suggestions will not only enhance cultural and civilizational dialogue, but also help resolve many of the conflicts that dot our landscape and mindset.

stories.headline: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.title: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.summary: Each previous instance coincided with extraordinary disruptions, from the Emergency and Lok Sabha dissolutions to Indira Gandhi’s assassination and the COVID-19 pandemic
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Winter Session of Parliament has been skipped only four times in India’s parliamentary history, and each instance was linked to exceptional circumstances, including the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

With the Monsoon Session yet to be prorogued, setting a record for Parliament remaining unprorogued for more than 100 days, speculation has grown over the possibility of a short special session to consider the delimitation Bill.
The absence of any move to summon Parliament for its customary winter sitting has also fuelled discussion about whether the session could be skipped altogether.
The first time Parliament missed its winter session was during the 19-month Emergency.
The Lok Sabha met from July 21 to August 7, 1975, and then only from January 5 to February 6, 1976, without sitting during November or December, when the Winter Session is normally held.
The next instance came in 1979 after the premature dissolution of the Sixth Lok Sabha on August 22.
The newly elected House met only in January 1980, resulting in the Winter Session being skipped.
A similar situation arose in 1984 following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31.
General elections were called, and the Eighth Lok Sabha held its first sitting on January 15, 1985.
After a gap of 36 years, the Winter Session was skipped again in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Amid fears over the spread of the virus and stringent social-distancing norms, Parliament did not meet after the truncated Monsoon Session that ran from September 14 to 23.
In the 12 years of the Narendra Modi government, the timing of the Winter Session has varied considerably.

stories.headline: Tata Steel acquires 2.77 crore APL Apollo Tubes shares worth Rs 5,825 crore in block deal; promoter S Gupta Holding pares stake
stories.title: Tata Steel acquires 2.77 crore APL Apollo Tubes shares worth Rs 5,825 crore in block deal; promoter S Gupta Holding pares stake
stories.summary: Tata Steel on Monday acquired 2,77,38,075 shares of APL Apollo Tubes worth around Rs 5,825 crore in a block deal from promoter group entity S Gupta Holding Private Limited, as the latter pared its stake in the company.According to BSE block deal data, Tata Steel purchased 69,34,519 shares and 2,08,03,556 shares of APL Apollo Tubes at Rs 2,100 apiece. S Gupta Holding Private Limited was the seller in the corresponding transactions, offloading an identical number of shares at the same price.Notably, S Gupta Holding Private Limited held 7,38,60,062 shares, representing 26.60% of APL Apollo Tubes' paid-up equity share capital, at the end of the September quarter of FY27, according to the company's exchange filing.Shares of APL Apollo Tubes settled at Rs 1,668.15 on Monday, down 21.39% from their previous close of Rs 2,122.15.ALSO READ: Bloodbath in APL Apollo shares: How much worse can the fall be and what should investors do?Earlier in the day, ahead of the block deals, APL Apollo Tubes had informed the stock exchanges that its board had approved the company becoming a party to a share purchase agreement dated November 23, 2026, between S Gupta Holding Private Limited, Tata Steel and the company.Under the agreement, S Gupta Holding will sell its entire holding of 7,38,60,062 equity shares, representing 26.38% of the company's equity share capital on a fully diluted basis, to Tata Steel in three tranches.The company said the first tranche of 2,77,38,075 shares was to be transferred through the stock exchange block deal window at Rs 2,100 per share. The second tranche comprises 3,33,19,009 shares, while the third tranche involves 1,28,02,978 shares. Both subsequent tranches are also priced at Rs 2,100 per share.APL Apollo clarified that it is neither a seller nor a purchaser under the agreement and that no consideration is payable to or by the company. Following the proposed acquisition, Tata Steel is required to make an open offer to acquire up to 7,28,06,387 fully paid-up equity shares, representing 26% of APL Apollo's expanded voting share capital, from public shareholders at Rs 2,301.40 per share, according to the exchange filing.APL Apollo’s investor presentation indicates that the company expects to raise debt of around Rs 28,000 crore to finance the acquisition, initially through acquisition financing before replacing it with long-term capitalisation. The additional leverage could weigh on the company’s balance sheet, interest costs and return ratios until the acquired businesses start contributing meaningfully to earnings.The valuation of the acquired businesses is another consideration. The Rs 28,000-crore transaction represents an enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple of around 24.8 times based on projected FY27 earnings, according to the company’s presentation. Investors will therefore look for clarity on the earnings contribution, integration benefits and the pace at which the debt can be brought down.

opening: Tata Steel on Monday acquired 2,77,38,075 shares of APL Apollo Tubes worth around Rs 5,825 crore in a block deal from promoter group entity S Gupta Holding Private Limited, as the latter pared its stake in the company.

body: S Gupta Holding Private Limited was the seller in the corresponding transactions, offloading an identical number of shares at the same price.

Notably, S Gupta Holding Private Limited held 7,38,60,062 shares, representing 26.60% of APL Apollo Tubes' paid-up equity share capital, at the end of the September quarter of FY27, according to the company's exchange filing.
ALSO READ: Bloodbath in APL Apollo shares: How much worse can the fall be and what should investors do?

Earlier in the day, ahead of the block deals, APL Apollo Tubes had informed the stock exchanges that its board had approved the company becoming a party to a share purchase agreement dated November 23, 2026, between S Gupta Holding Private Limited, Tata Steel and the company.
The company said the first tranche of 2,77,38,075 shares was to be transferred through the stock exchange block deal window at Rs 2,100 per share.
The second tranche comprises 3,33,19,009 shares, while the third tranche involves 1,28,02,978 shares.
Both subsequent tranches are also priced at Rs 2,100 per share.
APL Apollo clarified that it is neither a seller nor a purchaser under the agreement and that no consideration is payable to or by the company.

APL Apollo’s investor presentation indicates that the company expects to raise debt of around Rs 28,000 crore to finance the acquisition, initially through acquisition financing before replacing it with long-term capitalisation.
The additional leverage could weigh on the company’s balance sheet, interest costs and return ratios until the acquired businesses start contributing meaningfully to earnings.
The valuation of the acquired businesses is another consideration.
The Rs 28,000-crore transaction represents an enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple of around 24.8 times based on projected FY27 earnings, according to the company’s presentation.
Investors will therefore look for clarity on the earnings contribution, integration benefits and the pace at which the debt can be brought down.

stories.headline: When the Barracks Govern
stories.title: When the Barracks Govern
stories.summary: Pakistan has a prime minister, a two-chamber parliament, a Supreme Court, an election commission and, this summer, an election in PoK. What it cannot offer is a convincing answer to the oldest test of civilian rule: who can refuse the army, and what happens to them if they try? Three stories from the past year are usually told apart. A former prime minister petitions judges from a prison cell. A town in PoK sees an election season and a funeral season overlap. A court system is redrawn in under a week. I think they are one story, and I want to tell it that way. This is not a coup in the manner of 1958, 1977 or 1999. No general has dissolved the assembly, and Shehbaz Sharif is still prime minister. My argument is narrower and more unsettling. The informal tutelage scholars call “hybrid” rule is being turned into constitutional fact, and the generals are gaining something no past coup gave them: legal permanence. Start with the prisoner, because his case is easy to misread. Imran Khan is no constitutionalist saint. He came to power in 2018 with the military’s help and fell in 2022 when that help soured. His convictions in the Al-Qadir Trust and Toshakhana cases are now before the appellate courts, and the state calls them ordinary corruption cases. What troubles me is the pattern around them. His party was denied its election symbol before the 2024 vote, and its candidates still won more seats than anyone else as independents. The Supreme Court gave the party its reserved seats, then reversed itself, and the ruling coalition regained the two-thirds majority it used to rewrite the constitution. Civilians were tried by military courts after the 9 May 2023 riots. The army’s defenders have a case, and they deserve to be heard. The military’s spokesman calls Khan’s campaign against the institution a national-security matter and insists that the military is not the state. But note what the army chooses to punish. It court-martialled its own former spy chief, Faiz Hameed, partly for “political activities”. My reading is that politics is tolerated as an institutional prerogative and punished only when freelanced. The test is now concrete. Khan has written to the chief justices from jail describing isolation and failing eyesight. Officials dispute the details and say he is stable. Yet one fact is not in dispute. The Supreme Court ordered him moved to a private hospital in August, and months later it has not happened. An executive that can set aside an order of the highest court has answered the question of who is really obeyed. Compare this with the democracy I know. India is loud, quarrelsome and often maddening, but its institutions have a spine. Our courts strike down laws and rebuke ministers. Our press, for all its flaws, is large enough that no government can control it. Our generals salute the elected government and go back to their barracks, and nobody here seriously asks whether the army chief could remove the prime minister. Power in India changes hands because the voter decides it, not because a commission of appointees blesses the result. That contrast is sharpest in Kashmir. After 2019, the Indian state took a hard decision and then did something Pakistan has never done in PoK: it went back to the people. Assembly elections were held in Jammu and Kashmir in 2024, with strong participation, and an elected government took office. Violence is far below the peaks of the 1990s and 2000s, and visitors have returned in large numbers. The threat has not vanished, as the Pahalgam attack reminded us. A former prime minister petitions judges from a prison cell.
A town in PoK sees an election season and a funeral season overlap.
A court system is redrawn in under a week.
I think they are one story, and I want to tell it that way.
This is not a coup in the manner of 1958, 1977 or 1999.
No general has dissolved the assembly, and Shehbaz Sharif is still prime minister.
My argument is narrower and more unsettling.
The informal tutelage scholars call “hybrid” rule is being turned into constitutional fact, and the generals are gaining something no past coup gave them: legal permanence.
Start with the prisoner, because his case is easy to misread.
Imran Khan is no constitutionalist saint.
He came to power in 2018 with the military’s help and fell in 2022 when that help soured.
His convictions in the Al-Qadir Trust and Toshakhana cases are now before the appellate courts, and the state calls them ordinary corruption cases.
What troubles me is the pattern around them.
His party was denied its election symbol before the 2024 vote, and its candidates still won more seats than anyone else as independents.
The Supreme Court gave the party its reserved seats, then reversed itself, and the ruling coalition regained the two-thirds majority it used to rewrite the constitution.
Civilians were tried by military courts after the 9 May 2023 riots.
The army’s defenders have a case, and they deserve to be heard.
The military’s spokesman calls Khan’s campaign against the institution a national-security matter and insists that the military is not the state.
But note what the army chooses to punish.
It court-martialled its own former spy chief, Faiz Hameed, partly for “political activities”.
My reading is that politics is tolerated as an institutional prerogative and punished only when freelanced.
The test is now concrete.
Khan has written to the chief justices from jail describing isolation and failing eyesight.
Officials dispute the details and say he is stable.
Yet one fact is not in dispute.
The Supreme Court ordered him moved to a private hospital in August, and months later it has not happened.
An executive that can set aside an order of the highest court has answered the question of who is really obeyed.
Compare this with the democracy.
I know.
India is loud, quarrelsome and often maddening, but its institutions have a spine.
Our courts strike down laws and rebuke ministers.
Our press, for all its flaws, is large enough that no government can control it.
Our generals salute the elected government and go back to their barracks, and nobody here seriously asks whether the army chief could remove the prime minister.
Power in India changes hands because the voter decides it, not because a commission of appointees blesses the result.

stories.headline: Supreme Court flags ‘active connivance’ of civic authorities in ‘flagrant’ violations of building bye-laws
stories.title: Supreme Court flags ‘active connivance’ of civic authorities in ‘flagrant’ violations of building bye-laws
stories.summary: The court seeks suggestions from States and Union Territories on how to address such flagrant violations of building bye-laws
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 23, 2026) observed that unauthorised constructions often flourished with the “active connivance” of civic authorities in the hope that State governments would eventually regularise such structures, particularly ahead of elections.
The court sought suggestions from States and Union Territories on how to address such flagrant violations of building bye-laws.
“The state of municipal inspection in our cities, for example, is in shambles, to say the least.
It is often undertaken after the building has risen and the violation has become a fait accompli.
Such inspections are, to say the least, a sham.

It is also an open secret that unauthorised construction often flourishes with the active connivance of municipal authorities, hoping that State governments would ultimately regularise the same, particularly before an impending election,” a Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Sanjeev Sachdeva observed.
The Bench was hearing a case arising from Tamil Nadu concerning construction in violation of land-use norms and building bye-laws.
The proceedings had earlier been heard extensively by a Bench headed by Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, which had expanded the ambit of the case to examine similar violations across the country.

It had sought details from civic bodies in several State capitals on action taken against illegal constructions, besides issuing contempt notices to officials for failing to comply with its directions.
The case was, however, recently reassigned to the Bench headed by Justice Nagarathna following an administrative decision by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

Another public interest litigation, which arose from a private university student’s grievance, was subsequently expanded into a nationwide judicial inquiry on the functioning of private universities, including concessions granted to them, was also transferred from Justice Amanullah’s Bench.

On Monday (November 23, 2026), the Bench headed by Justice Nagarathna pointed to the “practical difficulties” of monitoring building bye-law violations nationwide, noting that differing regulations across States and Union Territories made it impractical to issue omnibus directions.

stories.headline: Supreme Court moots allowing only BS-VI-compliant vehicles into Delhi
stories.title: Supreme Court moots allowing only BS-VI-compliant vehicles into Delhi
stories.summary: The top court also stressed the need for a long-term plan to prevent polluting commercial vehicles from entering Delhi while ensuring uninterrupted supplies of essential commodities
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court orally mooted allowing only BS-VI or Bharat Stage 6 emissions norm-compliant vehicles into the national capital in a bid to curb air pollution on Monday (November 23, 2026).

Both the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) in the National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas and the Union Government identified vehicle emissions as one of the primary causes of the recurring pollution crisis in Delhi.

Justice Joymalya Bagchi, part of the three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, addressed the CAQM and the Centre, both represented by Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, and said the court would examine the question of restricting vehicular traffic in Delhi, if not the NCR, to only BS-VI vehicles.
BS-VI (Bharat Stage 6) vehicles are motor vehicles manufactured, sold and registered in India that comply with the strict emission standards introduced on April 1, 2020.
They align closely with Euro 6 norms and significantly cut harmful exhaust pollutants compared to older BS4 vehicles.
The top court also stressed the need for a long-term plan to prevent polluting commercial vehicles from entering Delhi while ensuring uninterrupted supplies of essential commodities.

Chief Justice Kant said that while the diesel trucks which form the bulk of the commercial traffic flowing into Delhi were a notorious source of pollution, Delhi would also suffer if there was an interruption in the flow of essential commodities like vegetables and fruits.
The court said a balance has to be struck between steps to reduce pollution and ensuring the free flow of necessities into the capital.
“Can there be warehouses installed at the borders, so that the goods could be brought into the city by battery-operated vehicles or non-polluting vehicles?
Such an arrangement may not be possible this year and may not be possible next year.
But why not have this in the next five years?
To ensure that not one commercial vehicle enters Delhi,” the CJI remarked.

stories.headline: CJI-led Bench Of Supreme Court To Hear Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam Bail Pleas On Nov 25
stories.title: CJI-led Bench Of Supreme Court To Hear Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam Bail Pleas On Nov 25
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court is set to hear bail pleas of former JNU scholar Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case after the Delhi High Court denied them bail recently.
A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana will hear the appeals on Wednesday(November 25).

It may be recalled that on January 5, 2026, a bench comprising Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice NV Anjaria denied bail to Imam and Khalid, calling them "ideological drivers" of the larger conspiracy.
It, however, granted bail to five other accused persons, including Gulfisha Fatima, by distinguishing the roles played by them in the alleged conspiracy.

While denying bail, the Court imposed a one-year embargo on the grant of bail and stated that Imam and Khalid can approach the Court upon the completion of protected witnesses' examination or upon expiry of 1 year from passing the order, "whichever is earlier".
The petitioners have filed the present appeal, submitting that the Supreme Court's one-year embargo imposed on the grant of bail is to expire soon.
They also said that the other condition imposed by the Court for examination of protected witnesses by the prosecution cannot possibly be completed by January 5, 2027.
Therefore, in light of prolonged incarceration, they be granted bail, the pleas urged.

stories.headline: India maps landslide susceptibility as part of shift from post-disaster relief to landslide management
stories.title: India maps landslide susceptibility as part of shift from post-disaster relief to landslide management
stories.summary: Mapping exercise covers 4.3 lakh square km; focus now on prevention, preparedness, risk reduction, says Science Minister; calls for interdisciplinary research, continuous monitoring to minimise impact
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India has completed a national landslide susceptibility mapping exercise across approximately 4.3 lakh square kilometres, while the landslide inventory database has compiled information on nearly 91,000 historical landslides by the end of 2025, Minister for Science and Technology Jitendra Singh said on Monday (November 23, 2026).

He noted that India is progressively shifting its approach to landslide management, from post-disaster relief to prevention, preparedness, and risk reduction, marking a “major transformation” in the country’s disaster management strategy.
He was speaking at the 7th World Landslide Forum being held at the Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Faridabad.
This is the first time the periodic International Consortium on Landslides and the International Programme on Landslides is being held in India.
The 4-day programme brought together international experts, scientists, and policymakers from more than 75 countries.

Recalling major landslide disasters in Kerala’s Wayanad and Uttarakhand’s Chamoli, as well as in Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh, and Jammu and Kashmir, Dr. Singh stressed the need for interdisciplinary research, continuous monitoring, and coordinated scientific efforts to minimise the impact of such disasters.

The National Landslide Forecasting Centre was established in Kolkata in 2024 and has now extended its activities to 20 districts, according to a statement from the Department of Science and Technology.
The Regional Landslide Forecasting System, established in 2020, is supporting experimental and operational forecasting across vulnerable regions, it added.

stories.headline: Climate change shared challenge for India, Nepal: President Murmu
stories.title: Climate change shared challenge for India, Nepal: President Murmu
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 23: Climate change shared challenge for India, Nepal: President Murmu President Droupadi Murmu on Monday said that climate change is a shared challenge for India and Nepal, and both the nations must work together to strengthen early warning systems and disaster management. In a meeting with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who called on her at the Rashtrapati Bhavan here, she said that the unique and multi-faceted bilateral relations between the two countries are based on their shared civilisational heritage and the deep cherished bonds between the people. The president expressed her condolences for the loss of life caused by the Bhotekoshi floods. She said that as always, in this difficult time, India has stood by Nepal, providing prompt humanitarian assistance and technical support, and will continue to do so as a close partner in the recovery and reconstruction efforts. The devastating Bhotekoshi floods that struck the Himalayan nation in August, killing at least 1,500 people and leaving over 5,000 missing, are estimated to have cost the country USD 4.7 billion in relief and reconstruction. Welcoming Prime Minister Shah, President Murmu congratulated him on the strong mandate for his government in the March 2026 elections, and wished him success in his efforts to fulfil the aspirations of the people. The president underlined that climate change is a shared challenge for both nations, and the two must work together to strengthen early warning systems and disaster management, according to a statement issued by her office. She said that the Joint Vision document announced during this visit reflects the aspirations of the people of both nations, especially the youth. President Murmu expressed confidence that it will provide a clear direction for our future cooperation in trade and investment, infrastructure, development partnership, connectivity, cultural and people-to-people exchanges, as well as in new and emerging sectors such as start-ups, digital services, space and innovation. Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced an economic package worth 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees for Nepal and flagged off a cross-border passenger train alongside his Nepalese counterpart Shah, as both sides finalised a vision document and signed eight pacts to deepen bilateral cooperation, signalling a major reset in ties after a spell of strain over their lingering boundary row.

She said that the Joint Vision document announced during this visit reflects the aspirations of the people of both nations, especially the youth.

President Murmu expressed confidence that it will provide a clear direction for our future cooperation in trade and investment, infrastructure, development partnership, connectivity, cultural and people-to-people exchanges, as well as in new and emerging sectors such as start-ups, digital services, space and innovation.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced an economic package worth 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees for Nepal and flagged off a cross-border passenger train alongside his Nepalese counterpart Shah, as both sides finalised a vision document and signed eight pacts to deepen bilateral cooperation, signalling a major reset in ties after a spell of strain over their lingering boundary row.
